patterns: short concrete real word with a product metaphor
altered familiar word that remains pronounceable
technical primitive with broad strategic meaning
craft metaphor that makes the user feel skilled
motion word implying speed without saying fast
visual word with clean identity potential
one or two syllables with crisp consonants
easy shell command that can be spoken aloud
real noun that gains depth from product context
precise adjective matching the product promise
balanced coined name with familiar roots
name that feels calm, durable, and confident
metaphor with both literal and technical readings
simple spelling with minimal pronunciation ambiguity
anti_patterns: generic SaaS suffixes like ify, ly, hub, stack, ops
names that describe the category too literally
cute mascot names without product seriousness
overlong names that fail as CLI commands
trend words that will age quickly
abstract optimism with no product metaphor
misspellings that create support or search friction
enterprise jargon posing as a brand
kill_rules: reject names that need a paragraph to justify
reject names containing AI unless the category requires it
reject names starting with Agent, Lang, Chain, Crew, Prompt, or Copilot
reject names longer than 10 letters unless exceptionally strong
reject names that are hard to pronounce on first sight
reject names with ambiguous spelling after hearing them aloud
reject names that feel like a Jira plugin or generic SaaS app
reject names that copy a competitor's structure too closely
reject names with weak filler suffixes such as ly, ify, io, base, hub, kit
reject names that cannot plausibly be a command-line binary
reject names with negative, fragile, slow, or chaotic associations
reject names whose metaphor conflicts with reliability or trust
reject names that feel trendy rather than durable
reject names that are only meaningful to insiders
preferred_shapes: hard consonant or bright vowel anchor

reference_lessons.name: Linear
reference_lessons.lesson: A familiar precision word can feel premium when it matches workflow clarity.

reference_lessons.name: Stripe
reference_lessons.lesson: Concrete nouns become powerful when they map to product rails and flow.

reference_lessons.name: Prisma
reference_lessons.lesson: Near-real coined names work when they carry visual structure and elegance.

reference_lessons.name: Temporal
reference_lessons.lesson: A serious technical primitive can own an infrastructure category.

reference_lessons.name: Dagster
reference_lessons.lesson: Developer-native roots can be friendly if the sound is approachable.

reference_lessons.name: Vercel
reference_lessons.lesson: Coined names need crisp phonetics and suggestive roots.

reference_lessons.name: Svelte
reference_lessons.lesson: A product promise embedded in a real adjective feels inevitable.

reference_lessons.name: Bun
reference_lessons.lesson: Extreme brevity can work when the product gives the name power.

reference_lessons.name: Raycast
reference_lessons.lesson: Technical metaphors with motion and precision feel native to builders.

reference_lessons.name: Tailscale
reference_lessons.lesson: Whimsy can coexist with infrastructure when the metaphor is concrete.

reference_lessons.name: Fly
reference_lessons.lesson: Short motion verbs are memorable, but broad terms need strong execution.

reference_lessons.name: Supabase
reference_lessons.lesson: Derivative clarity can help positioning but may cap distinctiveness.

reference_lessons.name: Turborepo
reference_lessons.lesson: Descriptive speed words work best for focused developer utilities.

reference_lessons.name: Playwright
reference_lessons.lesson: Craft metaphors can make automation feel intentional and skilled.
